The body keeps score in both directions: the mention of God moves the heart, and then it settles it. A humility that stopped at trembling would be alarm; the comfort is what makes it worship.

**The Second Mark: Endurance Without Commentary**

*Wa-l-ṣābirīna ʿalā mā aṣābahum* — and those who are patient over what befalls them. The preposition is *ʿalā*, which carries the sense of staying on top of something, holding one's place under a load.

This is the quality the sūrah's earlier figures conspicuously lacked. The man on the brink of verse 11 was content when good came to him and flipped over onto his face when a trial did; the man of verse 15 was consumed by rage at the delay of help.

The phrasing *mā aṣābahum* — whatever strikes them — is deliberately wide.

Sūrah al-Baqarah gives the patient their sentence, and the sentence explains the preposition: *“who, when faced with a disaster, say, ‘Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will ˹all˺ return’”* (2:156). Belonging stated, return faced — the staying-on-top that *ʿalā* describes is not stoicism but ownership acknowledged.

**Why the Humble Are Described Just Before the Fighting Begins**

The placement of this description is one of the sūrah's most deliberate choices, and it is easy to miss. Three verses from here, permission to fight will be granted (22:39), and the community that receives it is the community described here.

The order is a safeguard. A group that has been expelled from its homes and is about to be authorized to take up arms is first told what kind of people it is supposed to be: moved by the mention of God, patient under what befalls them, constant in prayer, open-handed with what they were given. Power is being granted to people whose defining marks are interior.

Read the other way round, the sequence is a warning. The sūrah is describing the people whose good news the Prophet is told to announce, and the next passage will describe what happens when a community is established in the land (22:41). The risk being guarded against is not defeat. It is the loss of the tremor.

**What the List Is For**

Read as a set, the four marks describe a shape rather than a checklist. The humble person is moved by the mention of God, stays in place under what happens to him, keeps the prayer up, and lets go of what he was given.

The order matters. The list begins inward and ends outward: a reaction, an endurance, an act of worship, an act of distribution. A person cannot start at the end of it — a generosity that does not come from the tremor is expenditure, and a prayer maintained without endurance is a habit that lasts as long as comfort does.

Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ states what the apparatus exists to produce, on the Day it is all that counts: *“Only those who come before Allah with a pure heart ˹will be saved˺”* (26:89). The four marks of verse 35 are that heart described while it is still in the world — trembling, enduring, praying, giving. The sacrifices of verses 28 to 37 were the outward machinery; this list is the product the machinery was built to make.

The same phenomenon is described elsewhere in the same physical vocabulary: *“which causes the skin ˹and hearts˺ of those who fear their Lord to tremble, then their skin and hearts soften at the mention of ˹the mercy of˺ Allah”* (39:23).

The Qur'an's opening portrait of the righteous joins the same two acts: *“who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them”* (2:3).
verses.36:
> We have made sacrificial camels ˹and cattle˺ among the symbols of Allah, in which there is ˹much˺ good for you. So pronounce the Name of Allah over them when they are lined up ˹for sacrifice˺. Once they have fallen ˹lifeless˺ on their sides, you may eat from their meat, and feed the needy—those who do not beg, and those who do. In this way We have subjected these ˹animals˺ to you so that you may be grateful

**Camels as Emblems**

*Wa-l-budna jaʿalnāhā lakum min shaʿāʾiri Allāhi* — and the sacrificial camels, We have made them for you among the emblems of God. The word *budn* refers to the large sacrificial animals; the jurists differed over whether it is restricted to camels or includes cattle, and both readings are defensible.

The classification is the point. An animal is being called a *shaʿīrah*, an emblem of God — the same word the sūrah used two verses before for the thing whose magnification comes from the reverence of hearts (22:32), and the same word used in Sūrah al-Baqarah for the two hills of Ṣafa and Marwah (2:158).

A camel is therefore in the same category as a hill: an ordinary creature that has been made to point at something. Nothing about the animal changes when it is dedicated. What changes is that it now carries a meaning, and the meaning is not the owner's to redefine.

Sūrah al-Baqarah applies the same word to the two hills of the pilgrimage walk: *“Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah”* (2:158). Hills and camels under one term — *shaʿāʾir* — which shows what the category holds: ordinary features of the world, stone and beast, taken up as pointers. The hill does not change when the pilgrim walks it, and the camel does not change when it is dedicated. Emblemhood is not a property added to the thing; it is a meaning the thing is made to carry.

**"In Them Is Good for You"**

*Lakum fīhā khayrun* — for you in them is good. The statement precedes the command to sacrifice, which is unusual and deliberate.

The animal is not being taken away. Before anything is demanded, the verse says that the arrangement benefits the person making it, and it says so in the widest available word — *khayr*, good, rather than any particular reward. The sūrah will repeat this structure in the verse after next, when it explains what actually reaches God.

Sūrah al-Naḥl itemises the good before any rite is mentioned: *“And He created the cattle for you as a source of warmth, food, and ˹many other˺ benefits”* (16:5). Warmth, food, benefits — the animal profitable to its owner in every direction before a single one is slaughtered. Verse 36's *lakum fīhā khayr* is that sentence recalled at the moment of sacrifice: the command to kill arrives only after the Creator has restated, in the widest word available, that the whole arrangement favours the giver.

**"When They Have Fallen on Their Sides"**

*Fa-idhā wajabat junūbuhā* — then when their sides have fallen, eat of them. Camels fall onto their sides when they are slaughtered, and the verse uses that as the marker of the moment after which the meat may be eaten.

The permission to eat was a correction of practice, as the commentators note: in the pre-Islamic period, some groups would not eat the meat of what they had sacrificed. The verse permits it, and the jurists drew the further ruling that eating is desirable rather than obligatory while feeding others is the binding part.

Sūrah al-Insān describes the feeding at its most costly, where the food is loved and given anyway: *“and give food — despite their desire for it — to the poor, the orphan, and the captive”* (76:8). Verse 36's asymmetry belongs to the same economy: the sacrificer permitted his share, the poor commanded theirs, and the binding part the part that leaves the household.

**"Thus We Have Subjected Them to You"**

*Ka-dhālika sakhkharnāhā lakum* — in that way We have made them subservient to you. The verb *sakhkhara* is used throughout the Qur'an for the created order placed at human disposal: *“He has subjected the ships for your service, sailing through the sea by His command”* (14:32), *“And He has subjected for your benefit the day and the night, the sun and the moon”* (16:12), and the same claim for animals, *“so that you may sit firmly on their backs, and remember your Lord’s blessings once you are settled on them”* (43:13).

The word carries an asymmetry: the subjected thing is stronger than the subject. A camel outweighs a man by a factor of six and could kill him; the sea is bigger than any ship. Subjugation here is a gift, not a conquest, and the verse draws the conclusion itself — *so that you may be grateful*.

Gratitude is the response the sūrah names, and it is the right one for a gift that the recipient did not arrange. A person who slaughters an animal that outweighs him, that could not have been subdued by force alone, and that he did not create, is being asked to notice what has been done for him.

The rule for eating is stated as a test of belief itself: *“So eat only of what is slaughtered in Allah's Name if you truly believe in His revelations”* (6:118).

Sūrah al-Baqarah describes the first kind in a passage that is almost a commentary on this phrase: *“˹Charity is˺ for the needy who are too engaged in the cause of Allah to move about in the land ˹for work˺. Those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not in need ˹of charity˺ because they do not beg”* (2:273).
verses.37:
> Neither their meat nor blood reaches Allah. Rather, it is your piety that reaches Him. This is how He has subjected them to you so that you may proclaim the greatness of Allah for what He has guided you to, and give good news to the good-doers

**God Is Not Fed**

The theological claim underneath the verse is the one the Qur'an makes with unusual bluntness elsewhere: God has no needs. A sacrifice that feeds the deity belongs to a religion of a different kind, and the Qur'an's insistence on this point is what makes its sacrificial law coherent.

If God were fed, the quality and quantity of the meat would be the variable that mattered, and the poor would be in competition with the altar. Because He is not, the meat has somewhere else to go, which is why the verse immediately before this one commanded that it be eaten and given away, and why the commentators ruled that feeding others is the binding part of the rite while eating is merely permitted.

The sacrifice is therefore not a transfer of goods upward. It is a distribution sideways, with the invocation as the thing directed upward.

Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt states the disclaimer in the first person: *“I seek no provision from them, nor do I need them to feed Me”* (51:57). No provision sought, no feeding needed — the two halves of every food-offering refused together. Verse 37 is that refusal applied to the sacrifice: the meat cannot be His portion because He takes no portion, which is why it is all available for the sideways distribution — eaten by the household, given to the poor — with nothing held back for heaven.

**The Address Switches to the Singular**

The last sentence of the verse changes grammatical person. Everything before has been plural — *your* piety, *He has subjected them to you* — and then the closing command, *give good news*, is addressed to a single person: the Prophet ﷺ.

The switch is not a slip and the commentators noted it. The ruling in the first half of the verse is for the community; the announcement in the second half is the Prophet's office. He is the one who gives good news, and the sūrah marks that by changing the grammar rather than by naming him.

The same shift happened in verse 34, which also ended with *give good news*, and the two are a pair: good news to the humble, and good news to the good-doers.

The office is defined where the Prophet's limits are drawn: *“We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire”* (2:119). Good news and warning as the whole commission, accountability for results explicitly removed. The singular *bashshir* in verses 34 and 37 is that office exercised: the community receives the ruling in the plural, and the Prophet alone is told to announce its happy ending.

**"That You May Magnify God for Guiding You"**

*Li-tukabbirū Allāha ʿalā mā hadākum* — so that you magnify God for the guidance He gave you. The purpose of the whole arrangement is stated here, and it is not the transfer of anything.

The object of gratitude is *hudā*, guidance. The animal, the subjugation, the slaughter and the meal are all secondary to the fact that these people were shown what to do. A religion that begins with being guided will always owe its central act to the guidance rather than to the offering.

The verb is *kabbirū*, to declare great — the same root as the *takbīr* that opens the prayer and accompanies the slaughter. Magnification is not praise for a benefit received; it is the acknowledgment of the size of the One who gave it.

The formula recurs where another pillar closes, and the occasion shows what it is for: *“so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful”* (2:185). *Li-tukabbirū Allāha ʿalā mā hadākum* — the same words, closing Ramaḍān as they close the sacrifice. Fasting completed, pilgrimage offered, and both sealed with magnification *for the guidance* rather than for the strength to perform: the rite is received before it is performed, and the takbīr confesses the order.

**Good News to the Good-Doers**

*Wa-bashshir al-muḥsinīna* — and give good news to the good-doers. *Iḥsān* is the word for doing a thing well, for excellence that exceeds the requirement.

The sūrah's last word on the sacrifice is thus addressed to a quality of character rather than to a rite. The people who are promised good news are not the ones who slaughtered, since the sūrah has just said the slaughter itself arrives nowhere. They are the ones for whom the slaughter was an act of *iḥsān* — done properly, for the right reason, with the meat reaching the people it was meant for.

Sūrah al-Naḥl closes on the company the good-doers keep: *“Surely Allah is with those who shun evil and who do good ˹deeds˺”* (16:128). With-ness as the reward of *iḥsān* — not payment rendered but presence granted. The good news of verse 37 is that presence announced in advance: the slaughter done properly, for the right reason, with the meat reaching its people, places the doer where God is with him, which is the only arrival the verse promises.

Sūrah Fāṭir names what does ascend, and the cargo is exactly what verse 37 allows: *“To Him ˹alone˺ good words ascend, and righteous deeds are raised up by Him”* (35:10).
verses.38:
> Indeed, Allah defends those who believe. Surely Allah does not like whoever is deceitful, ungrateful

**The Root Shared With Verse 40**

The word used here reappears two verses later in the famous statement that had God not repelled some people by means of others, monasteries and synagogues and mosques would have been destroyed.

The repetition ties the two verses into a single principle.

The principle is stated as general history in Sūrah al-Baqarah, in the aftermath of David and Goliath: *“Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another, corruption would have dominated the earth, but Allah is Gracious to all”* (2:251). The same *dafʿ*, the same unnamed agents, the same counterfactual — what is preserved there is the earth from corruption, what is preserved here is the believers from their persecutors and worship from destruction.

**"God Loves Not Every Treacherous Ingrate"**

*Inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu kulla khawwānin kafūr* — God does not love any treacherous, ungrateful person. Two vices are named in one phrase, and they belong together.

*Khawwān* is the intensive form: a person given to betrayal, for whom treachery is a habit rather than a lapse. *Kafūr* is likewise intensive — not merely ungrateful but a denier of what he has been given. The pairing describes a character rather than an act: the man who betrays trusts and then denies that he was ever trusted with anything.

The Qur'an states the same judgement elsewhere in almost the same words, which confirms that this is a standing principle rather than a remark about one group.

The same verdict is pronounced where treachery is most tempting — in the handling of treaties with a party expected to break them: *“And if you ˹O Prophet˺ see signs of betrayal by a people, respond by openly terminating your treaty with them. Surely Allah does not like those who betray”* (8:58). Even anticipating the other side's betrayal does not license one's own; the instruction is to end openly, in daylight, rather than to answer secret breach with secret breach. Verse 38 is that ruling stated as a principle before the permission arrives.

**Why This Verse Precedes the Permission to Fight**

The commentators report an occasion that makes the sequence intelligible. Some believers still in Makkah, suffering persecution, wanted to respond with treacherous methods — assassination, deception — and the revelation answered first with this verse and then, in verse 39, with permission to fight openly.

That sequence is the whole moral structure of the passage, and it is worth stating as clearly as the text does. The permission to use force is granted one verse *after* the prohibition of treachery, which means the permission arrives already bounded. You may fight; you may not betray.

The report also explains why the second vice is ingratitude. A person who has been wronged and concludes that he is therefore free of the rules is denying the good he received — including the good of being forbidden to deceive.

Sūrah al-Māʾidah states the boundary in its most demanding form: *“Do not let the hatred of a people lead you to injustice. Be just! That is closer to righteousness”* (5:8). The hatred is not denied — the believers hated their persecutors with reason — but it is disqualified as a ground for action. That is the same structure as verses 38 and 39 taken together: the injury is real, the permission is granted, and the hatred the injury produced is not permitted to write the rules of the response.

**Treachery Has No Good Ends**

The temptation the verse addresses is the most durable one in political ethics: that a just cause licenses unjust means, and that the urgency of the situation suspends the ordinary prohibitions.

The Qur'an's answer is structural rather than consequentialist. It does not argue that treachery fails, though it often does; it states that God does not love the treacherous, which settles the matter regardless of outcome. A victory obtained by betrayal is not reclassified as righteous by its result.

The tradition recorded a corresponding image for the Day of Resurrection, and the report al-Qurṭubī cites is a well-attested one. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A flag will be fixed on the Day of Resurrection for every betrayer, and it will be announced, 'This is the betrayal of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so.'" It is recorded in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* (6178, and again at 6966).

The image is exact. Betrayal is a hidden act — that is what makes it betrayal — and the punishment announced for it is that it will be made public, with the betrayer's name and his father's name attached to it. The thing he did in secret becomes the thing he is known by in front of everyone.

The prohibition's positive form is the keeping of pledges: *“Honour Allah's covenant when you make a pledge, and do not break your oaths after confirming them, having made Allah your guarantor”* (16:91).
verses.39:
> Permission ˹to fight back˺ is ˹hereby˺ granted to those being fought, for they have been wronged. And Allah is truly Most Capable of helping them ˹prevail˺

**The Verse That Changed the Community's Posture**

*Udhina li-alladhīna yuqātalūna bi-annahum ẓulimū* — permission is granted to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged.

This is the verse most often identified as the first to authorize the believers to use force. Before it, the community's instructed response to persecution had been patience and withdrawal, and twice that withdrawal had taken the form of emigration: a small group to Abyssinia in 615, under the protection of the Christian Negus, and then the emigration of the Prophet and his companions from Makkah to Madīnah in 622.

Some place its revelation at the point of the Hijrah itself, and al-Qurṭubī records that when Abū Bakr heard it he remarked that he had known all along that combat would eventually be permitted. Al-Ṭabarī connects it instead with a party of believers who set out to leave Makkah, were intercepted and turned back by their persecutors, and were then granted leave to resist.

**The Grammar of Permission**

*Udhina* is a passive verb with no agent named. Nobody is doing the permitting in the sentence, which is the standard Qur'anic way of attributing an authorisation to God without making Him the subject of a finite verb.

The word matters more than it looks. What is granted is permission — *idhn* — not obligation and not enthusiasm. A command would have made fighting a duty of the same order as the prayer; a mere concession would have implied it was tolerated but regrettable. Permission sits precisely between them: it is lawful, it is not mandatory on every individual, and it is not celebrated.

That is the register the whole passage keeps. The sūrah has just forbidden treachery (22:38) and will immediately state the grievance that justifies the fighting (22:40) and the conditions attached to the power it may produce (22:41). Nothing here is a licence.

The passive is also how the Qur'an normally attributes acts of authorisation to God. A named subject would have made the sentence a piece of legislation among others; the agentless *udhina* presents it as something lifted — a restraint that had been in place and is now removed. The community is not being told to do something new so much as being told that what it had been forbidden to do is no longer forbidden.

**"Those Who Are Being Fought"**

The participle is passive: *yuqātalūna*, those who are fought against.

The grammar establishes the sequence, and the sequence is the justification. These people are not aggressors who have been granted a blessing on their aggression; they are the objects of force who have been allowed to stop being only objects. The passive participle carries the whole moral asymmetry of the verse in a single word.

This is why the verse is so often cited in discussions of the Islamic law of war. The permission is not attached to disbelief, to proximity, or to any quality of the opponent. It is attached to the fact of being attacked.

The restriction to the party that was attacked is stated as law elsewhere, and the wording leaves no room for extension: *“Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Surely Allah does not like transgressors”* (2:190). The permission of this verse and the limit of that one are the same ruling seen from two sides: the object of force may respond, and the response has a ceiling.

**Why the Permission Falls Inside a Pilgrimage Sūrah**

The placement is worth a moment, because it looks like a digression and is not. This is the sūrah of the pilgrimage — the sūrah that was named for the rite its audience had been prevented from performing, and that declared the Sacred Mosque open to resident and visitor alike (22:25).

The people being granted permission to fight are the people who were barred from the House. The passage that follows will state the grievance in a sentence: they were expelled for saying that their Lord is God. What is being authorized is the recovery of a community's ability to worship where it was told to worship, and the authorisation is bounded by that.

That is why the sūrah can move from verses about sacrificial camels to verses about armed defence without any sense of incongruity. Both are about a community that has been prevented from practising its religion, and both are permissions granted to people who had been told to wait.

The sūrah has already said what the Mosque is for: it was made open to the resident and the visitor alike, and whoever intends to profane it in deviation will be made to taste a painful punishment (22:25). Those are the terms in which the fighting is authorised. The people who were kept out of the House by force are being permitted to remove the force, and nothing broader than that is licensed by the verse.
verses.40:
> ˹They are˺ those who have been expelled from their homes for no reason other than proclaiming: “Our Lord is Allah.” Had Allah not repelled ˹the aggression of˺ some people by means of others, destruction would have surely claimed monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which Allah’s Name is often mentioned. Allah will certainly help those who stand up for Him. Allah is truly All-Powerful, Almighty

**The Grievance, Stated in One Sentence**

*Alladhīna ukhrijū min diyārihim bi-ghayri ḥaqqin illā an yaqūlū rabbunā Allāh* — those who were driven out of their homes without any right, except that they say, "Our Lord is God.".

The offence for which these people were expelled was a sentence. Not a raid, not a theft, not a sedition: a creed stated aloud. The verse frames it that way because the framing is the argument. Whatever else the Quraysh believed they were doing, the charge against the believers reduces to a claim about who God is.

The exception particle *illā* does the work: they were expelled for nothing *except* saying this. A person can be lawfully expelled for a crime; there is no lawful expulsion for a sentence of worship.

The same expulsion was plotted against the Prophet himself, and Sūrah al-Anfāl names all three options his opponents weighed: *“when the disbelievers conspired to capture, kill, or exile you”* (8:30). Capture, killing, exile — the sentence of verse 40 records which of the three was carried out against the community. The verse's *illā* — for nothing except saying *our Lord is God* — is what turns the exile from a political fact into the paradigm injury: no crime preceded it, so no justification can follow it.

**The Expulsion Was the Grievance the Qur'an Cited Most**

The commentators note that this grievance is among the most frequently cited in the Qur'an against the Quraysh. The same expulsion is named in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where it is the ground of the permission to fight: *“Kill them wherever you come upon them and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out. For persecution is far worse than killing”* (2:191).

The repetition matters legally as well as rhetorically. In the Qur'anic framework, expulsion from one's home for one's religion is not one injury among many; it is the paradigm injury, and the permission granted in verse 39 is tied to it specifically rather than to hostility in general.

Sūrah al-Baqarah ranks the expulsion above fighting in the sacred months, in a verse that weighs the two directly: *“hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing”* (2:217). The expulsion from the Mosque is not only listed among the injuries; it is placed on the scale against a violation the audience already regarded as grave, and found heavier. That ranking is what makes verse 40's grievance the ground of verse 39's permission.

**"Had God Not Repelled Some People by Others"**

*Wa-law-lā dafʿu Allāhi al-nāsa baʿḍahum bi-baʿḍin* — and were it not for God's repelling of people, some of them by means of others.

The principle is a sober one. The world is not preserved by the victory of the good; it is preserved by a balance of restraint in which aggression is met and checked. The agents in the sentence are unnamed and undifferentiated: *some people by means of others*. Nobody is assigned the role of the righteous party.

This is the same root the sūrah used in verse 38 for God's defence of the believers, and the two are one doctrine. God pushes back against aggression through whatever and whoever He wills, and the survival of anything fragile — a community, a building, a rite — is the result.

Sūrah Hūd states the counterfactual from the other side — what happens where no restraint exists: *“If only there had been among the ˹destroyed˺ peoples before you virtuous individuals who forbade corruption in the land — other than the few We had saved”* (11:116). The destroyed peoples are described as lacking exactly what verse 40 describes God supplying: a check, a resistance, a party that pushes back. Where the repelling is absent the corruption runs to its end; where it is present — through whomsoever God wills — monasteries and mosques alike survive it.

**"God Will Help Those Who Help Him"**

*Wa-la-yanṣuranna Allāhu man yanṣuruhu* — God will certainly help whoever helps Him.

The phrasing is deliberately paradoxical. God has no need of help, and the commentators resolve it in the obvious way: helping God means helping His religion and His messenger.

The paradox carries a warning, though. "Helping God" can be claimed by anyone with a cause, and the sūrah has just specified what it means in this case: standing up for a religion whose followers were expelled for saying that their Lord is God, and whose defence includes the buildings of other people's worship. Any other claim to be helping Him is not covered by this promise.

The verse closes with two names — *qawiyy*, strong, and *ʿazīz*, mighty — and the point of closing there is that the help promised does not depend on the strength of the people being helped.

Sūrah Muḥammad states the same promise as a direct address to the believers, with the mechanism named: *“O believers! If you stand up for Allah, He will help you and make your steps firm”* (47:7). Standing up, help given, steps made firm — the promise of verse 40 with its middle term supplied. The help is not described as victory in the field but as firmness of step, which is the form divine help takes for a community that has just been told its victory is God's to give (22:39) and its defence is God's own act (22:38).

The general reading of *masājid* has a verse that supports it directly: *“The places of worship are ˹only˺ for Allah, so do not invoke anyone besides Him”* (72:18).
verses.41:
> ˹They are˺ those who, if established in the land by Us, would perform prayer, pay alms-tax, encourage what is good, and forbid what is evil. And with Allah rests the outcome of all affairs

**Power Is Described as Something Granted**

*Alladhīna in makkannahum fī al-arḍi* — those who, if We establish them in the land. The verb is *makkannā*, from *makkana*: to give someone a firm place, to put him in a position where he can act.

The subject of that verb is God. These people do not seize power; they are established in it. That is the first thing the sūrah says about the community that has just been authorized to fight, and it is the frame for everything that follows. A community that wins is not a community that has taken something; it is a community that has been placed, and the placing is conditional on what it does there.

Joseph is the Qur'an's worked example of the same verb: *“This is how We established Joseph in the land to settle wherever he pleased”* (12:56). A man sold into slavery, imprisoned on a false charge, and then placed where he could act — the establishment arrives as a grant after utter powerlessness, not as the consolidation of a victory. The verse's closing clause is the one this sūrah's audience needed: the reward of the good-doers is never discounted, which means the interval of powerlessness was not a loss.

**The Sentence Is a Conditional, Not a Prediction**

*In makkannahum* — if We establish them. The particle is a condition, and a condition can go unmet.

The sūrah is being realistic here, and the realism is part of the instruction. Power is described as a possibility that God may grant, not as a promise already made; the community reading this verse in Makkah had no sovereignty and no certainty of obtaining any. What they are told is what would be expected of them if it came.

The conditional also removes any suggestion that the fighting permission of verses 39 and 40 was a grant of territory. It was leave to resist an expulsion. Whether those resisting would ever be established in the land is left open in the grammar, and the conditionality is what keeps the four duties from reading as a programme for conquest.

The conditional has a counterpart in Sūrah al-Nūr, where the same establishment is stated as a promise with its condition attached: *“Allah has promised those of you who believe and do good that He will certainly make them successors in the land … ˹provided that˺ they worship Me, associating nothing with Me”* (24:55). Promise and condition travel together — succession granted, worship stipulated. Verse 41 here is the same structure with the four acts filling in what the worship looks like once the promise is kept.

**The Fourth Item Is the Dangerous One**

Forbidding wrong is the item that gets communities into trouble, and the sūrah names it without qualification.

The reason is that the alternative is worse. A community that prays, pays and keeps to itself has abandoned the public character of the religion it was expelled for saying out loud — the very sentence for which these people lost their homes was a public claim about God.

The tradition's discussions of *al-amr bi-l-maʿrūf* focus almost entirely on its limits and etiquette — who may do it, when, and by what means — which is the recognition that the fourth item is the one that requires judgement.

Sūrah Āl ʿImrān does not lay the fourth item on every individual as a personal license; it lays it on *a group among* the community: *“Let there be a group among you who call ˹others˺ to goodness, encourage what is good, and forbid what is evil — it is they who will be successful”* (3:104).

**Who Is Being Described**

The commentators proposed several referents. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī took the verse as describing the conditions laid on whoever God establishes in the land, meaning those given sovereignty. Others took it as a description of the Emigrants specifically, or of the Muslims generally.

The first reading has the most to recommend it, because the verse's grammar is a conditional: *if* We establish them. A conditional describes what follows from a condition rather than what a named group happens to do. Whoever holds power is being told what the power was given for.

Read that way, the verse is a standing criterion rather than a historical description, and it applies to the community in every generation in which it has been established — including the generations in which it was an empire.

The conditional reading has a named precedent. David was told what his establishment was for in the same terms: *“O David! We have surely made you an authority in the land, so judge between people with truth. And do not follow ˹your˺ desires or they will lead you astray from Allah's Way”* (38:26). Authority granted, purpose stipulated, desire warned against — the three elements of verse 41 in a single address to a king. Whoever holds power stands where David stood, under the same instruction.

Sūrah Āl ʿImrān makes the same acts the definition of the community's rank: *“You are the best community ever raised for humanity — you encourage good, forbid evil, and believe in Allah”* (3:110).

Moses stated the same closing clause to a people with no power at all: *“Seek Allah's help and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah ˹alone˺. He grants it to whoever He chooses of His servants. The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous”* (7:128).
verses.42:
> If they deny you ˹O Prophet˺, so did the people of Noah before them, as well as ˹the tribes of˺ ’Ȃd and Thamûd

**Denial Is Presented as the Pattern, Not the Emergency**

*Wa-in yukadhdhibūka fa-qad kadhdhabat qablahum qawmu Nūḥin* — and if they deny you, the people of Noah denied before them.

The conditional is doing something specific. It does not say "when they deny you" and it does not say "since they have denied you." It says *if*, and the apodosis is not a threat but a precedent. The verse's first move is to reclassify the Prophet's situation: this is not a crisis, it is the norm.

That is the Qur'an's most consistent consolation to its messenger, and it appears in the same form elsewhere: *“If they deny you, so did those before them. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, divine Books, and enlightening Scriptures”* (35:25). The point is never that rejection is easy. It is that rejection is what happens to messengers, and that a messenger who is being rejected is not by this failing.

Sūrah al-Anʿām adds what the precedent cost and what it produced: *“Indeed, messengers before you were rejected but patiently endured rejection and persecution until Our help came to them. And Allah's promise ˹to help˺ is never broken”* (6:34). Rejection, endurance, help — the three are presented as a sequence with the middle term supplied by the messenger. The consolation is therefore not that denial is unreal but that it is the first term of a completed pattern, and the help at the end of it is promised rather than merely hoped for.

**The List That Follows Is Arabian**

The three names given here — Noah, ʿĀd and Thamūd — are the three the Qur'an most often uses as the opening of this catalogue.

The choice is rhetorical rather than chronological. ʿĀd and Thamūd were the Arabian peoples whose destruction was part of the peninsula's inherited memory; their ruined settlements were places a traveller could point at. By putting them beside Noah, whose flood was known through the scriptural traditions of the region, the verse builds a list that its first audience could not dismiss as foreign folklore.

Sūrah Ibrāhīm uses the same opening for the same purpose: *“Have you not ˹already˺ received the stories of those who were before you: the people of Noah, ’Âd, Thamûd, and those after them? Only Allah knows how many they were”* (14:9).

Thamūd's dwellings were the most visible item on the route the audience travelled: *“Indeed, the residents of the Stone Valley also denied the messengers”* (15:80). The Stone Valley — al-Ḥijr, the carved facades the Syrian caravans passed — is named as a place rather than only a people, which is what makes the list unanswerable for its first hearers. Noah belongs to transmitted memory; ʿĀd and Thamūd belong to the road the merchants walked twice a year, with the houses of the destroyed still standing in the rock.

**What Was Denied Was a Messenger**

The verb throughout is *kadhdhaba*, to declare someone a liar — the verb of refusing a person rather than refusing a proposition.

This matters for how the catalogue functions. The parallel is not between the Makkans' theology and the theology of ʿĀd; the parallel is between the Makkans' treatment of their messenger and the treatment of Hūd, Ṣāliḥ and Shuʿayb. Sūrah Hūd records what each of them said, and the message is identical in every case: *“And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd. He said, ‘O my people! Worship Allah. You have no god other than Him’”* (11:50).

The offence, in other words, is not rejecting an unfamiliar doctrine. It is calling your brother a liar when he tells you something true.

Noah's sentence is recorded in the same words Hūd used: *“Indeed, We sent Noah to his people. He said, ‘O my people! Worship Allah — you have no other god except Him’”* (7:59). The first messenger on the list and the Arabian ones spoke one sentence with different names attached, which is what makes the catalogue a single charge rather than nine different ones. What was denied in every case was the same claim from a brother's mouth — and what the Makkans were denying was that same sentence again.

**Why the Prophet Is Told This Now**

The placement of the catalogue matters. It follows the permission to fight, and that is the moment at which a community might reasonably conclude that it has been vindicated and that the reckoning is about to begin.

Verses 42 to 48 are the correction to that expectation. The pattern in history is not that the truthful are vindicated quickly; it is that the deniers are given time and then seized. The Prophet is being told, before he fights his first battle, that the schedule is not his and that the delay is not a sign of anything.

The delay is then given its universal form, and the verse that states it removes the last comfort of the denier: *“If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for their wrongdoing, He would not have left a single living being on earth. But He delays them for an appointed term”* (16:61). The silence the Makkans were enjoying was not a verdict in their favour but the same deferral extended to everyone, including the believers. To be inside the interval is not to be acquitted; it is to be given an appointed term, which expires whether or not anyone is watching the clock.
verses.43:
> the people of Abraham, the people of Lot

**Lot's People and the Nature of Their Refusal**

Lot's community is the one item on the list whose specific crime is reported in detail elsewhere in the Qur'an, and it was not idolatry in the ordinary sense.

Their denial took the form of refusing a prohibition, assaulting the guests in their town, and treating the messenger who warned them as an offender. They are described as a people who *transgressed* rather than as a people who worshipped stones, and their destruction was correspondingly specific: the town was turned upside down and rained with stones of baked clay.

Including them widens what the catalogue covers. The list is not a catalogue of polytheists. It is a catalogue of communities that were told something by a messenger and refused it, whatever form the refusal took.

The destruction is described with a specificity the catalogue form deliberately withholds here: *“And We turned the cities ˹of Sodom and Gomorrah˺ upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay”* (15:74). Inversion from below and bombardment from above — the town assaulted in both directions at once. The compression of verse 43 is doing the opposite work: it reduces that detailed catastrophe to two words of a list, because the catalogue's argument runs on number rather than on horror.

**What "His People" Means for the Verdict**

The phrase *qawmu Ibrāhīma* — the people of Abraham — is the standard Qur'anic formula for the community a messenger was sent to, and its assumptions repay attention.

The assumption is that a messenger is sent *to* someone. No messenger in the Qur'an preaches to humanity in the abstract; each is sent to a specific people with a specific language. The universal address of verse 49 will come later in this passage, and it is the exception that proves the rule.

The consequence for the catalogue is that the rejection is always local and particular. These communities were not rejecting a distant message; they were rejecting a message delivered to them, in their language, by one of their own, and that is what makes the verdict on them intelligible.

The rule is stated as a principle of revelation itself: *“We have not sent a messenger except in the language of his people to clarify ˹the message˺ for them”* (14:4). Language here means more than vocabulary — it means the whole shared world of kinship, custom and reference inside which a claim can be understood. That is what makes the rejection on this list a refusal rather than a misunderstanding: each community was addressed in the idiom it thought in, by a man it had watched grow up.

**Every Messenger on This List Was an Insider**

One feature runs through the whole catalogue and is easy to miss because the verses are so compressed. Every messenger named was sent to *his own* people, and the Qur'an is careful to say so.

*“And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ”* (7:73). *“And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd”* (11:50). The word translated "brother" is used repeatedly and with emphasis: Shuʿayb is called the brother of the people of Midian (7:85), and the pattern holds for every community on the list.

The significance for the consolation being offered is considerable. These communities were not rejecting foreigners with unfamiliar customs. They were rejecting a man they had grown up with, whose family they knew, whose honesty they had previously relied on. The denial was not a failure of information about the messenger; it was a refusal to accept a claim from someone whose ordinariness was the problem.

That is precisely the objection the Qur'an records against Muhammad ﷺ — that he was a man like them, that he ate and walked in the market, and that no angel had been sent down with him. The catalogue's answer is that this has always been the arrangement.

**Why the Kaʿbah's Neighbours Should Have Recognised This**

One further consideration. Abraham's people and Lot's people were the communities nearest to the audience's own geography, and their ruins were known. ʿĀd and Thamūd were in the peninsula; Lot's towns were on the trade route to Syria that Makkah's caravans used every year.

The Qur'an's argument here is not addressed to people who needed to be told these stories for the first time. It is addressed to people who passed the remains on their way to work, and who are being asked why the remains did not change their minds.

Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt makes the geographical point explicit, and it is addressed to the same audience: *“You ˹Meccans˺ certainly pass by their ruins day and night. Will you not then understand?”* (37:137–138). Twice daily — the caravans went out in the morning and came back at night past the same remains. The ruins were not a destination requiring a journey but a sightline on the commute, which is why the verse treats the failure as one of understanding rather than of information.

The household link is stated as a conversion: *“So Lot believed in him. And Abraham said, ‘I am emigrating ˹in obedience˺ to my Lord’”* (29:26).
verses.44:
> and the residents of Midian. And Moses was denied ˹too˺. But I delayed ˹the fate of˺ the disbelievers ˹until their appointed time˺ then seized them. And how severe was My response

**Midian and Its Messenger**

The catalogue closes with the people of Midian, to whom the Qur'an sent Shuʿayb. The account is preserved in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf: *“And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib. He said, ‘O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord. So give just measure and weight, do not defraud people of their property, nor spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order’”* (7:85).

Midian is the last community on the list whose messenger is named in the Qur'an by name besides the five already given, and it is the one whose offence was economic — fraudulent measures, commercial cheating — which broadens the catalogue again. These are not all idolaters, and they are not all guilty of the same thing. What they share is the refusal.

**"But I Granted the Disbelievers Respite"**

*Thumma akhadhtuhum* is preceded by *fa-amlaytu li-l-kāfirīn* — I gave the disbelievers respite. The verb *amlā* means to give rein, to let run on, to allow more length.

This is the sentence the whole catalogue was building toward, and it is the point the sūrah needed to make at this juncture. Nine communities were named, and the thing said about all of them is that they were given time. The delay is not an oversight or a reprieve; it is the standing procedure.

The sūrah has been preparing this since verse 1. The Hour is *coming* (22:7) rather than arrived; Iblīs was *delayed* in the parallel sūrahs; the man who wanted the punishment hurried is told in the next verse that a day with God is a thousand years. Delay is the sūrah's most consistent claim about how God runs the world, and this verse states it as a matter of history.

**"Then I Seized Them"**

*Thumma akhadhtuhum* — then I took them. The verb is plain and physical, and *thumma* places it after an interval of unspecified length.

The combination is what makes the verse frightening, and it is the same combination the sūrah opposed in verse 40 to the aggression of the Quraysh. Wrongdoing is met, but not on the schedule the wronged party would choose. The delay is long enough for the deniers to conclude that nothing is coming.

The suddenness is the point, and the Qur'an states it as a rule rather than as a detail of these nine cases: *“˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed! Our torment took them by surprise ˹while sleeping˺ at night or midday”* (7:4). The seizure arrives in the middle of ordinary life, at the hour when a community is least expecting it — which is what makes the interval preceding it so misleading to the people inside it. Length followed by suddenness is one pattern, not two events.

**"And How Was My Denial"**

*Fa-kayfa kāna nakīr* — and how was My *nakīr*? The word is the verse's difficulty, and the commentators recorded two readings of it.

*Nakīr* comes from the root *n-k-r*, which gives both "to deny" and "to disapprove, to alter something into a state one dislikes." On the first reading the phrase means "how was My denial of them" — God's rejection answering theirs, the same word used for their refusal. On the second it means "how was My rebuke," or "how terrible was the change I wrought.".

Both senses are present in the Arabic, and the ambiguity is a deliberate piece of lexical justice. They denied; the response is described with the same root. The punishment is named as a matching refusal rather than as an unrelated act of force. The same closing question appears elsewhere in the Qur'an in the same form, which confirms that the phrase is a fixed formula: *“Then I seized those who persisted in disbelief. How severe was My response!”* (35:26). The whole catalogue of verses 42 to 44 comes down to two verbs at the end: *amlaytu*, I gave rein, and *akhadhtu*, I took.

Everything else in those three verses is a list of names. The sūrah is not interested in the differences between the communities — their different sins, their different messengers, their different centuries.

The community reading this verse in Makkah was, in the sūrah's telling, in the first half of the sequence.
verses.45:
> Many are the societies We have destroyed for persisting in wrongdoing, leaving them in total ruin. ˹Many are˺ also the abandoned wells and lofty palaces

**"How Many a Town"**

*Wa-ka-ayyin min qaryatin ahlaknāhā* — and how many a town did We destroy. The construction *ka-ayyin* is the Arabic idiom for an uncounted large number, and it is always used in the Qur'an to introduce a claim that could be documented but will not be enumerated.

The rhetorical effect depends on the reader supplying the number. A text that said "seven towns" would be making a historical claim that could be checked and disputed. A text that says *how many* is making a claim about the character of history itself, and it invites the audience to count for themselves from what they have seen.

**"Fallen Upon Its Roofs"**

*Fa-hiya khāwiyatun ʿalā ʿurūshihā* — so it lies hollow upon its roofs. The image is an inversion, and al-Rāzī explained the sequence: the roofs collapsed first, and then the walls fell on top of them, leaving the structure lying on what used to be its uppermost part.

The detail is the kind of thing only someone who has walked through a ruined town would say. A building destroyed from the outside leaves walls standing and rubble at the base; a building whose roof goes first ends up inside-out. The verse is describing the specific look of a place that has been abandoned for a long time.

The word *khāwiya* — hollow, empty, collapsed inward — carries the desolation. What is being described is not a ruined building but a town that used to be full and is now a shell lying on itself.

The ruined town is used elsewhere as the site of a resurrection argument, and the picture is the same one: *“Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. He wondered, ‘How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?’”* (2:259). What the ruins provoke in both places is the same question about whether what is over is finally over — and in this sūrah the answer is directed at the living rather than the dead.

**The Argument Is Empirical**

The Qur'an's appeal here is to evidence, and it is worth being precise about what kind.

The ruined settlements of the peninsula were not known to the Makkans from books. They were on the trade routes. Caravans passed them, watered at some of the wells, and told stories about them. The verse asks its audience to do the arithmetic: this many towns, all destroyed, all of them in a state of wrong at the time.

Sūrah al-Rūm draws the conclusion the Qur'an draws from this evidence: *“Have they not travelled throughout the land to see what was the end of those ˹destroyed˺ before them? They were far superior in might; they cultivated the land and developed it more than these ˹Meccans˺ ever have. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. Allah would have never wronged them, but it was they who wronged themselves”* (30:9).

Note the last clause. The evidence from the ruins is not that God is harsh; it is that the destruction was self-inflicted. Nothing in the record suggests that a town was taken while it was behaving well.

**Why the Ruins Did Not Settle the Question**

The next verse will say what follows from all this, and it is the harder claim: the evidence was available and did not produce the conclusion. Travelling through the ruins is not sufficient, because travelling is done with the eyes.

The next verse supplies the diagnosis, and it is the harder claim of the two. The ruins are on the trade routes and everyone has seen them; what is missing is not evidence but the faculty that reads it. Sūrah Muḥammad puts the same question in the same words, and the complaint is that the travelling happened and the learning did not: *“Have they not travelled throughout the land to see what was the end of those before them? Allah annihilated them, and a similar fate awaits the disbelievers”* (47:10).

Verse 46 will say that it is not the eyes that are blind but the hearts in the breasts, and the sequence matters: the evidence is already in front of the audience, so the remaining problem cannot be evidential.
verses.46:
> Have they not travelled throughout the land so their hearts may reason, and their ears may listen? Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind

**The Question Assumes the Answer Is No**

*A-fa-lam yasīrū fī al-arḍi* — have they not travelled in the land? The interrogative expects a negative answer only in the rhetorical sense: of course they have travelled. The Quraysh were merchants; their caravans went to Syria in the summer and to Yemen in the winter, and the routes passed directly through the ruins of the communities named in the previous verses.

So the question is not whether they moved about. It is whether the moving about did what moving about is supposed to do. The sūrah has just described abandoned wells and lofty palaces lying on their roofs; this verse asks why passing them produced nothing.

The audience's travelling was not incidental to them; it was the basis of their prosperity. A sūrah of the Qur'an is addressed to Quraysh precisely in those terms — their security and their two annual caravans, to Yemen in the winter and to Syria in the summer (106:1–2). The routes those caravans took ran past the ruins named in verses 42 to 44. The question therefore lands on people who had passed the evidence twice a year for their entire commercial lives and had drawn nothing from it.

**"It Is Not the Eyes That Go Blind"**

*Fa-innahā lā taʿmā al-abṣāru* — for it is not the eyesights that are blind. The word *abṣār* is the plural of *baṣar*, eyesight or insight, and the verse denies the defect there.

The denial is the verse's centre. The problem with these people is not a failure of observation. They saw the ruins, they saw the wells, and they saw that the towns were empty. Their eyes worked perfectly. What failed was the step from seeing to concluding.

That is a diagnosis of a specific and common condition: the evidence is in front of a person and produces nothing, because the person has no framework that would make it mean something. Adding more evidence would not help. What is missing is the organ that weighs it.

Sūrah al-Aʿrāf states the condition in its fullest form, and the organ is the same one: *“Indeed, We have destined many jinn and humans for Hell. They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with. They are like cattle”* (7:179). The failure is not a missing faculty but an unused one, which is why the same sūrahs can describe these people as having hearts, eyes and ears and still say that they do not perceive.

**"But the Hearts Which Are in the Breasts"**

*Wa-lākin taʿmā al-qulūbu allatī fī al-ṣudūr* — but blind are the hearts that are in the breasts.

The phrase *allatī fī al-ṣudūr*, which are in the breasts, looks redundant and is not. It is there to insist that the heart in question is the physical organ in a person's chest and not a poetic abstraction. The Qur'an's anthropology locates understanding in a real thing inside a real body, and it says so to prevent the reader from spiritualising the diagnosis away.

The same insistence appears in a well-known ḥadīth. Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: "In the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the entire body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the entire body is corrupt — it is the heart." It is recorded in *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī* (52) and *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* (1599). The report's logic is the verse's logic: the condition of the whole person follows the condition of a particular organ.

The question the Qur'an poses about the Qur'an is posed in the same vocabulary, and it places the fault in the same organ: *“Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Or are there locks upon their hearts?”* (47:24). The lock image and the blindness image are the same diagnosis from two directions — the apparatus is intact and the reception is not happening, so the defect must be in the receiver.

**What the Verse Requires of a Traveller**

The purpose clause is explicit: travel *so that* hearts reason and ears hear. The Qur'an is not commending travel for its own sake and is certainly not commending curiosity about old stones.

That qualification matters, because travel of exactly this kind was familiar to the audience. The caravans passed the ruins every year and the guides told stories about them, and nothing about the arrangement produced a change. What is being demanded is not more miles but a different kind of attention: the willingness to let what is seen count as evidence about oneself rather than as entertainment.

The sūrahs that repeat this appeal frame it identically, as a demand to see *the end of those before them* rather than merely their remains: *“Say, ‘Travel throughout the land and see the fate of the deniers’”* (6:11), and *“Similar situations came to pass before you, so travel throughout the land and see the fate of the deniers”* (3:137). The object of the seeing is always a conclusion, never a sight.

The demand is therefore not for travel but for a particular posture towards what travel produces. The sūrah's own audience had the miles and lacked the posture, which is why the verse is framed as a question about their own experience rather than as an instruction to go anywhere. They had already been to the ruins. What they had not done was let the ruins be about them.
verses.47:
> They challenge you ˹O Prophet˺ to hasten the torment. And Allah will never fail in His promise. But a day with your Lord is indeed like a thousand years by your counting

**The Taunt**

*Wa-yastaʿjilūnaka bi-l-ʿadhābi* — and they ask you to hurry the punishment. The verb is the intensive form of "to hasten": they keep asking, and the asking is a form of mockery rather than a request for information.

The demand appears repeatedly in the Qur'an, always in the same key. The opponents do not say that the punishment is unjust; they say it is late, and they treat the lateness as evidence that it is not coming. The challenge is designed to be unanswerable: a messenger who produces the punishment looks vindictive, and a messenger who does not produce it looks mistaken.

The demand is recorded elsewhere in the same words, and in Makkah it was once phrased as a prayer: *"O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment"* (8:32). Sūrah Yūnus supplies the answer the demand invites: *"Imagine if His torment were to overcome you by night or day—do the wicked realize what they are ˹really˺ asking Him to hasten? Will you believe in it only after it has overtaken you? Now? But you always wanted to hasten it!"* (10:50–51). The reply exposes the request as something other than a request for evidence. A punishment that arrives is the end of the period in which evidence could be answered at all, and the taunt is therefore a demand that the testing be brought to a close.

**"A Day With Your Lord Is Like a Thousand Years"**

*Wa-inna yawman ʿinda rabbika ka-alfi sanatin mimmā taʿuddūna* — and a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.

The commentators proposed several referents. Some took the day as one of the six days of creation mentioned elsewhere in the Qur'an, comparing it with the statement that a day with God measures a thousand years by human reckoning (32:5). Others took it as one of the days of the Hereafter, meaning the Day of Resurrection or the day of reckoning itself. Al-Rāzī recorded a further reading: that a day of punishment will *feel* to the sufferer like a thousand years, so the delay is not the point — the duration, once it begins, is.

The figure has a larger neighbour that the commentators had to reconcile with it: *"˹through which˺ the angels and the ˹holy˺ spirit will ascend to Him on a Day fifty thousand years in length"* (70:4). Their answers differed — that the thousand and the fifty thousand describe different days, or different experiences of one day, or the reckoning as a whole against a single stage of it — but they agreed on what the numbers are doing. Neither is being offered as a measurement. Both are the largest available figures pushed against a duration that has no human equivalent, and the argument of the verse is unaffected by which reading is taken.

**The Taunt's Own Logic**

There is a further point the Qur'an makes about demands of this kind, and it is worth stating here because it completes the answer. A person demanding the punishment as a proof would not be satisfied by it if it came, because the demand is not really for evidence.

The sūrah has already said as much about the Hour: once the signs arrive, believing does nothing for a person who did not believe before (6:158). The demand to hurry the punishment is, structurally, a demand that God settle the question in a way that removes the need for faith — and the whole design of the testing period is that the question is *not* settled that way.

The delay the mockers cite against the Prophet is the same delay that keeps them alive to object. *"If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for their wrongdoing, He would not have left a single living being on earth. But He delays them for an appointed term"* (16:61). The respite is not a gap in the system; it is the system. Every day of it is a day in which the objection can still be withdrawn, and the taunt is an argument against the very arrangement that makes the taunter's existence possible.

**What the Verse Does for the Prophet**

The practical effect of the verse is to remove the taunt's sting. A messenger told that a day with God is a thousand years is not being told that his opponents will wait a long time for punishment. He is being told that the delay he is mocked for is not a delay at all from the only vantage point that counts.

What he is given is not a date. It would be a misreading to hear the verse as "wait a little longer," because nothing in it promises that the wait will be short measured in his years — and the sūrah will go on to describe a community that emigrates, fights, and is tested long before it returns to the sanctuary (22:39–41, 22:58).

That is the same consolation the catalogue of verses 42 to 44 offered from the other side: the deniers were given length, and then they were taken.

The same claim about God appears on the other side of the argument, in the prayer of the believers: *"Our Lord! You will certainly gather all humanity for the ˹promised˺ Day—about which there is no doubt. Surely Allah does not break His promise"* (3:9).
verses.48:
> Many are the societies whose end We delayed while they did wrong, then seized them. And to Me is the final return

**The Verse Restates Verse 45 With One Word Changed**

*Wa-ka-ayyin min qaryatin amlaytu lahā wa-hiya ẓālimatun thumma akhadhtuhā* — and how many a town did I grant respite while it was doing wrong, then I seized it.

The sentence is almost identical to verse 45, and the difference is one verb. Verse 45 said *ahlaknāhā*, We destroyed it. Verse 48 says *amlaytu lahā*, I gave it rein. The destruction is still there, at the end, but the emphasis has moved from the end to the interval.

This is a deliberate repetition with a purpose, and recognising the purpose is the key to the passage. Verse 45 established that destruction happens. Verse 48 establishes what happens in between: a length of time, granted by God, during which the wrongdoing continued and nothing appeared to be done about it.

The pronoun shifts with the verb. The act of granting time is attributed personally to God, and the sūrah will do the same two clauses later, where the destination is likewise *to Me*.

**Delay as a Deliberate Act**

The verb *amlā* is significant. It is the word for letting out a rope, for giving an animal more rein, for allowing someone to continue without interruption. It describes a decision rather than an oversight.

That has a consequence for how the interval is read. The centuries during which a wrongdoing community flourished were not a period in which God was unaware or unable. They were granted. The Qur'an has a technical term for this condition and a doctrine built on it — the drawing-on of a person by stages, while he interprets the silence as approval.

Sūrah al-Anʿām states the mechanism: *“When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair!”* (6:44). The gifts keep arriving, the warnings stop feeling urgent, and the recipient concludes that the silence of heaven is a verdict.

**"Then I Seized It"**

*Thumma akhadhtuhā* — then I took it. As in verse 44, the verb is plain and the *thumma* marks an interval whose length is not stated.

The pairing of the two clauses is the whole doctrine: a long silence, then a single action. The sūrah is describing the same pattern it has described three times already — in the respite granted to the deniers of verse 44, in the Hour that is coming rather than arrived (22:7), and now here.

For the audience in Makkah, the application was direct and uncomfortable. They were, at that moment, inside the interval. The town they lived in was prosperous, the trade routes were working, and nothing had happened to them. The verse's point is that this is exactly what the interval before the seizure looks like, in every recorded case.

The interval is not described as a period of improvement. The wrongdoing continued through it — *wa-hiya ẓālimatun* is circumstantial here as it was in verse 45 — which means the respite was granted while the thing that provoked the seizure was still being done.

**Why the Repetition Is Not Redundancy**

A reader in a hurry will see verses 45 and 48 as the same verse twice, and will be wrong. Verse 45 was addressed to the evidence: look at what is left of them. Verse 48 is addressed to the objection: they were given time, and you are being given time.

The two are answering different questions. The first answers "does God destroy communities?" The second answers "then why is nothing happening?" — which is precisely the question the previous verse recorded being thrown at the Prophet.

The two questions are asked by two different people. The first is the question of a reader looking at evidence and wondering whether the pattern is real; the second is the question of a person living inside the interval and wondering whether the pattern applies to him. The sūrah answers both, and the order matters — a community that has accepted that God destroys towns has still to accept that the silence it is currently enjoying is the same silence that preceded every destruction on the list.
verses.49:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O humanity! I am only sent to you with a clear warning

**The Prophet Is Told What to Say About Himself**

*Qul yā ayyuhā al-nāsu innamā anā lakum nadhīrun mubīn* — Say: O humanity, I am only, for you, a clear warner.

The verse begins with the imperative *qul*, say. The Qur'an uses this formula when it wants the Prophet to announce something in the first person, and what he is told to announce here is a description of his own office rather than a doctrine.

That is itself a claim worth noticing. The message is not "say that God is one" or "say that the Hour is coming." It is "say what you are." The audience has been demanding signs, hurrying the punishment, and disputing about the messenger, and the response is a statement of job description.

The same imperative opens the comparable definitions elsewhere, and the repetition tells the reader that this is a fixed reply to a fixed objection. When the disbelievers ask why no sign comes down, the answer given to the Prophet is: *"You ˹O Prophet˺ are only a warner. And every people had a guide"* (13:7). When he is told to state the limits of his own knowledge, the answer takes the same shape: *"Say, 'I have no power to benefit or protect myself, except by the Will of Allah… I am only a warner and deliverer of good news for those who believe'"* (7:188). The office is defined by the imperative in every case, as though the definition were something the Prophet needed to hear as much as his opponents did.

**What a Warner Is Not**

The Qur'an is consistent about the limits of the office, and the consistency is the point. A *nadhīr* warns: he tells people what is coming and what the consequences are. He does not compel, he does not settle disputes by force, and he is not responsible for whether anyone listens.

Those limits are not a diminution of the role. They are what make the warning a moral act rather than a threat.

The Qur'an states the exemption in so many words: *"We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire"* (2:119).

**Why the Warning Must Be "Clear"**

*Mubīn* means clear, evident, manifest — the same adjective the sūrah used for the verses sent down in 22:16 and for the scripture the disputant lacked in 22:8.

Clarity is a moral requirement in the Qur'an, not a stylistic preference. A warning that could reasonably be misunderstood leaves the person warned with an excuse, and the entire edifice of judgment requires that no one has one. The messengers were sent with clear proofs and clear warnings for exactly that reason.

This is also why the clarity is attributed to the warning rather than to the warner. It is not that the Prophet is an especially lucid man; it is that what he brought is unambiguous about what is being asked and what is being threatened.

**A Refrain on Many Messengers' Lips**

The formula is not unique to Muhammad ﷺ, and the Qur'an puts it into the mouths of the messengers whose communities were just listed. Noah says it, Hūd says it, Ṣāliḥ says it, Shuʿayb says it, and the Prophet is told to say it in the same words.

The repetition across the sūrahs is a claim about the unity of the message rather than a literary device. Every messenger brought the same thing: a warning, clearly stated, to his own people. The variations were in what each community did about it.

The same unity is stated from God's side in the verse that gives the purpose of sending them at all: *"We have sent messengers only as deliverers of good news and as warners. Whoever believes and does good, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"* (6:48). The two functions are named together there, as they are in 7:188, and the pairing is the reason the office has the shape it has: good news can be refused, and a warning can be heeded, and neither of those is possible unless the recipient is left free.

**The Address Is the Widest One Available**

The same formula with which this sūrah opened (22:1), and it is not the formula most of the Medinan passages use.

The choice is deliberate and it matches the claim being made. The Prophet is not being told to announce his office to a tribe, a city or a community of followers. He is being told to announce it to everyone, which is consistent with the sūrah's opening move of addressing the Hour to all humanity rather than to a congregation.

It is also consistent with the verse that appears earlier in this sūrah in which God is described as judging between all the communities by name (22:17). The message goes out to the same breadth as the judgment will cover.
verses.50:
> So those who believe and do good will have forgiveness and an honourable provision

**"A Noble Provision"**

*Wa-rizqun karīm* — and a noble provision. The adjective is *karīm*, a word with a wide field: generous, noble, honourable, plentiful, fine.

The range matters, because the promise is not that the provision will be large. *Karīm* describes the manner of the giving at least as much as the quantity given. A provision that is *karīm* is given generously, by a giver who is not counting, in a way that honours the recipient rather than merely sustaining him.

The same pairing appears elsewhere in the Qur'an in the same formula, which confirms that this is a standing description of the reward rather than a phrase coined for this verse. What is promised to the believers is not a wage computed against their works; it is provision given in the manner of a generous host.

The formula is not the sūrah's own. It appears in almost these words in Sūrah al-Anfāl, attached to a description of the believers' character: *“It is they who are the true believers. They will have elevated ranks, forgiveness, and an honourable provision from their Lord”* (8:4). The recurrence is what settles the meaning: this is the standing vocabulary of the reward, and *karīm* is doing the same work in both places — describing the standing of the recipient as much as the size of the gift.

**The Third Statement of This Promise**

This is the sūrah's third formulation of the believers' reward, and the repetition is worth tracking rather than skipping. Verse 14 gave the Gardens with rivers beneath them. Verse 23 added the bracelets of gold and the silk. Verse 50 gives forgiveness and a noble provision.

The three are not competing accounts. They describe the same thing from three directions: location (the Garden), honour (the adornment), and relationship (forgiveness, then provision). Together they cover what a person could want from a reward — somewhere to be, dignity, and a settled account.

The sequence is also a progression, and it runs inward. Verse 14 names a location, verse 23 names an adornment, and verse 50 names a relationship — an account settled and a table set. A reward described only as a place could in principle be given to a person who was still at odds with the giver. The third formulation rules that out.

**Provision, Not Wages**

The word is *rizq*, provision — the same word used for the sacrificial animals in verses 28 and 34, and for what the believers spend from in verse 35. It is not a word for payment.

That distinction carries weight in a sūrah that has been insistent about grace. Verse 14 said God *admits* the believers to the Gardens; verse 23 said they are *adorned*, passively; and this verse offers provision rather than remuneration. Nothing in the sūrah's vocabulary of reward suggests a transaction that God is settling.

The practical consequence is that the reward is not proportioned to the works, and the verse does not invite anyone to compute it. Karīm provision is what a generous giver gives, and what he gives is his to determine.

The word's range elsewhere confirms the reading. Provision in the Qur'an is what God gives to creatures who have done nothing to earn it: *“There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah”* (11:6). To make the reward *rizq* rather than a wage is to place the believers' recompense in the same category as the sustenance of everything that lives — given, guaranteed, and not negotiated.

**What the Verse Does Not Say**

The verse also declines two things that readers regularly add to it.

It does not say the provision is in the Hereafter only. The word is unqualified, and the Qur'an uses the same phrase for what God gives in this life as well as the next; the promise is not dated.

And it does not say that the believers will be spared suffering in the interval. The sūrah has just described a community authorized to fight after being expelled from its homes, and it will describe martyrs in verse 58. What is promised is forgiveness and a noble provision, and neither is a promise that the interval will be comfortable.

That omission is itself part of the sūrah's honesty. A promise of ease would have been contradicted within a generation, and the Qur'an does not make promises that experience can falsify. What it promises is that the account is settled and the provision will come — neither of which is the same as comfort.

There is a third omission worth naming. The verse does not say that the two halves come separately, or that the provision is deferred in its entirety to the Hereafter. Read in a sūrah that has just promised to settle the believers in a land and establish their religion (22:41), the promise sits naturally across both lives, and the sūrah is content to leave the dating open.
verses.51:
> But those who strive to discredit Our revelations, they will be the residents of the Hellfire.”

**Not Disbelief but Campaigning**

*Wa-alladhīna saʿaw fī āyātinā muʿājizīna* — and those who strove against Our signs, seeking to frustrate.

The verb *saʿā* means to strive, to exert oneself, to work at something with effort. It is the same verb used for a person running to the prayer or working for a livelihood. What is described here is not a state of unbelief but an expenditure of energy.

That is the verse's target, and it is narrower and more serious than simple denial. A person can disbelieve passively, and the Qur'an treats that as one thing. This verse describes people who work at it: who organize, argue, mock, and spend their days trying to make the signs ineffective.

The same imperative is addressed to the believers about the Friday prayer: *"O believers! When the call to prayer is made on Friday, then proceed ˹diligently˺ to the remembrance of Allah and leave off ˹your˺ business"* (62:9).

**What the Campaign Looked Like**
